parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A man phones a company to arrange a carpet-cleaning visit to his house.
script: Good morning, Fernbank Carpet Care, Clara speaking. How can I help you?
Oh, good morning. I'd like to arrange for someone to come and clean the carpets in my house, please.
Of course. I'll just take a few details first. Could I have your surname?
Could you spell that for me?
Lovely, thank you, Mr Lindqvist. And your address?
It's 27 Foxglove Lane. That's F-O-X-G-L-O-V-E, Lane.
Yes, just behind the old mill.
Got it. And a contact number?
07712 640 983. Thank you. Now, which areas would you like cleaned?

Well, I was going to have the bedrooms done as well, but I've decided to leave those for now. So it's mainly the lounge and the hall. And the stairs, to be honest. They're the worst of all, because everybody walks up and down them in their outdoor shoes.
So the lounge, the hall and the stairs. And is there any particular problem I should note down for the technician?

Yes, there's a big stain in the lounge. My nephew knocked over a glass of red wine at the weekend. I did try to deal with it myself, with a damp cloth and then some salt, but it's still there. Oh, and there's a coffee mark near the door as well, but that's quite old and faint.
Right, red wine. We have a special treatment for that, so I'll add it to the booking. Is it a wool carpet?
Yes, I think so. It was here when I moved in.
That's fine. We use a gentle method for wool. Now, when would suit you? We could send someone on Tuesday the 12th.
Hmm, I can't do the 12th, I'm at work all day. Is Thursday possible?
Let me see. No, I'm afraid Thursday the 14th is full. The next day I have is Tuesday the 19th.
The 19th? Yes, I'm off that day, so that's fine.
Wonderful. And would you prefer the morning or the afternoon? We've got a slot at 10.30 or one at 1.30.
Oh, the morning's no good for me, I have to do the school run and I'd never be back in time. Make it the afternoon, then. 1.30 is fine.

Perfect. Now, I can give you the price. We charge by area. The lounge is 65 pounds, the hall is 38 pounds and the stairs are 45 pounds. The stain treatment is an extra 9 pounds 50. If you'd wanted the bedrooms done, they would have been 40 pounds each.
So what does that come to altogether?

One more thing. Our technicians will move chairs and small tables, and there will be two of them, so they can manage a sofa. But they can't lift very heavy furniture. Is there anything large in the lounge?
There's the sofa, and there's a big bookcase against the wall. It's full of books.
The sofa will be no problem, but the bookcase is too heavy for them, I'm afraid. Could you empty it and move it away from the wall before we arrive?
Of course. I'll ask my neighbour to give me a hand.
Thank you. And how would you like to pay? Most people use a card, and we can take that on the day.
I'd usually do that, but my card has just expired and the new one hasn't arrived. Could I pay by cheque, if that's all right?
Yes, that's absolutely fine. Just make it payable to Fernbank Carpet Care.
Will do. Is there anything else I need to know?
Only that the technician will phone about twenty minutes before arriving. We'll see you on the 19th, Mr Lindqvist. Goodbye.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: A farmer gives visitors a briefing at the start of a tour of a working dairy farm.
script: Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to Bramble Hill Dairy Farm. My name's Hamish, and I'll be taking you round this afternoon. Before we set off, I'd like to give you a quick briefing, so you know what to expect and what we ask of you.

First, a little about the farm. My great-grandfather bought this land nearly a hundred years ago, and my family has run it ever since. We started offering tours about eight years ago. Now, the extra income does help, of course, but that wasn't the main reason. What really made us do it was that so many children, and quite a few adults, had never seen where their milk comes from. We wanted people to see how food is actually produced, and to ask questions.

So, the cows. We have 280 altogether. When my grandfather started, he had about eighty. Normally around 210 of them are in milk at any one time, but at this time of year a lot of the herd is resting before calving, so only 140 are being milked right now. You'll see the rest out on the hill.

Our tour lasts about two hours, and we'll visit five places in this order. The first is the calf shed. We keep the newborn calves there for their first eight weeks. Because young calves catch infections very easily, everyone has to wash their hands at the sinks by the door before going in. It only takes a minute, and there's soap and paper towels, so please don't skip it.

From the calf shed, we'll go to the milking parlour. The afternoon milking starts at 3.30, and the schedule says we'll be there at 4 o'clock. But the vet is visiting this afternoon, so we'll do the calf shed first and that pushes things back, so we'll actually reach the parlour at half past four, when the milking is in full swing. It's a noisy place, and the cows are easily startled. So you're welcome to take photographs, but please switch your flash off. A sudden flash can upset a whole row of cows and make them kick.

Now, the milk. Most of it, about four fifths, is collected every second day by a large dairy company, and I'm afraid I don't know where it ends up. The rest we turn into cheese here on the farm, and that's our next stop. In the cheese room, the staff have to keep everything very clean, so for hygiene reasons you'll be given a paper hairnet at the door. Yes, even the gentlemen with no hair at all. You'll see the cheese being turned and the big copper vats, and at the end, there's a small tasting.

After that, we walk across to the hay barn. This is where we store winter feed, and it's also where the tractors and the big machinery are kept. They come in and out all the time, and drivers can't always see small people, so I'd ask parents to keep young children by the hand while we're in there. By the way, there's a yellow line painted on the floor beside the slurry pit, which we pass on the way. Please stay behind it. It's not a nice place to fall.

Our last stop is the meadow trail, which goes along the stream and up the hill. It's a gentle walk of about twenty minutes, but the ground can be very muddy, and cow pats are everywhere. If you haven't brought boots, don't worry, we have wellingtons in all sizes in the porch, so please put a pair on before we leave the yard. You'll be glad you did.

A few more practical points. Some visitors ask what happens if it rains. We don't cancel, and we don't shorten the tour either. Cows don't mind a bit of weather, and there are covered walkways between most of the buildings. Waterproof jackets are a good idea, though. Also, in the paddock beside the barn we have two goats and a donkey. Please don't feed them. They've all got strict diets, and even a handful of the wrong thing can make them ill.

Finally, when we get back to the yard, there's the farm shop, which sells our cheese, eggs and ice cream, and there's a cafe next door for tea and cake. It closes at 5.30, so don't leave it too late. Right, if there are no questions, let's get going. Follow me, and mind the step on your way out.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two journalism students, Callum and Ingrid, compare their internship experiences at local newspapers.
script: Hi, Ingrid. Have you managed to start the report on our newspaper placements yet?
Hardly. I thought we could compare our experiences first, since the report is supposed to be reflective. You were at the Ashburn Courier, weren't you?
That's right. And you were at the Merrow Gazette.
Yes. Funny, you'd applied to the Gazette too, hadn't you?

I did. It has that reputation for investigative stories, and it's ten minutes from my flat, so on paper it was the obvious choice. But then Dev, who did his placement at the Courier last year, told me that interns there actually get stories printed under their own name. That settled it.
Did he turn out to be right?
He did. By week three I had my first byline. What about you? Was the Gazette what you expected?

Not at all. I imagined shouting and phones ringing, like in the films. But it's a big open-plan room where you could hear a pin drop. Everyone sits with headphones on, typing. For the first few days I was almost afraid to cough.
Well, the Courier was busier. Though it's quite a small team, so you don't feel lost.
Same here. What was the first thing they asked you to do? I spent a whole day just reading old issues.

They'd warned me I'd be answering readers' calls, and I was dreading it, but that didn't start until the second week. My first task was writing headlines and picture captions for the website. They gave me about thirty, and the sub-editor rewrote nearly all of them.

Ouch. Which brings me to the thing I want to put in the report. People say the most important thing an intern learns is to write quickly, but I could already do that. And checking facts was drilled into us at university, so that wasn't new either.
So what was it for you?

Accepting criticism. I used to take it personally when my editor crossed out whole paragraphs. Now I see each correction as a free lesson, and honestly my writing has improved more in six weeks than in a year of seminars.
I think that's true for me too, although I'd say the deadlines were the biggest change.
Right. Now, what should the report actually focus on? Dr Perera said we could choose. I wondered about how the newspapers select their interns.
I thought of that, but the handbook says the report has to be about what we learned. What about the website and how the paper is changing?
That's more of a project than a placement report, I think. Look, here it says reflect on the skills you developed. So that's what we should do. Skills it is.
Agreed. And maybe we could add a section of practical tips for next year's interns. That's always useful.
Good idea. I'll start. Obviously, tell them to bring a spare phone charger. Yours died at a council meeting, didn't it?
Yes, and I had to borrow a stranger's. Embarrassing. Okay, what else? You'd say practise shorthand, wouldn't you?
Definitely. I could only manage about half the speed I needed and I missed some quotes. If they can learn it over the summer, they'll be well ahead.
Then there's the feedback. Tell them to ask the features editor on Fridays. She has time then, whereas the news editor is always rushing.
And never leave the office without your press pass. I was nearly refused entry to a school sports day because I'd left mine on my desk.
Right. That's four. Shall we do the writing up this week? When's the deadline?
Dr Perera said Wednesday at the start, but then she emailed to say it had been moved to Friday, so we have a bit longer. She wants it uploaded by five o'clock.
Friday, then. Let's meet on Monday to go through the first draft.
Perfect. I'll send you my notes tonight.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecturer talks about fungi and the networks they form in forests.
script: Good morning, everyone. Today I want to talk about fungi, and in particular about the part they play in the life of a forest. Most people think of a mushroom as a small plant that grows from the ground, but that is a misunderstanding on two counts. First, fungi are not plants. In fact, if we look at their DNA, they are more closely related to animals than they are to plants. Second, the mushroom itself is only a small part of the organism. It is simply the fruiting body, the equivalent of an apple on a tree, and it exists to release spores.

The real body of a fungus lies hidden underground. It is made of fine threads, called hyphae, which are so thin that you cannot see a single one without a microscope. These threads grow outwards and branch again and again, and together they form a mass called a mycelium. To give you an idea of how much of this there is, a single teaspoon of healthy forest soil can contain up to 200 metres of these threads, and the mycelium of some species can cover several square kilometres.

So what are all these threads doing? Well, for most of the fungi we are interested in today, the answer is that they are partners of trees. We call this partnership mycorrhiza, which simply means fungus-root. The fungal threads wrap around, or even enter, the tips of tree roots. Now, a tree's roots can only reach so far, but the threads of the fungus can go much further and into much smaller spaces in the soil. So the fungus acts as an extension of the root system, collecting water and minerals that the tree could not reach alone. In particular, it provides phosphorus, which is scarce in many soils, as well as nitrogen.

In return, the tree gives the fungus sugars, which it makes by photosynthesis. In some forests, trees may pass on as much as a third of the sugars they produce. It's a very expensive arrangement for the tree, but one which pays off. Most of the trees you see around you today could not survive without it, and about nine out of ten land plants form some kind of partnership of this sort.

Now, here's where the story becomes more interesting. Because one fungus can connect to the roots of many different trees at once, the trees become linked together in a kind of underground network. Experiments suggest that substances can travel through these links from one tree to another. For example, young seedlings growing in deep shade, where they receive very little light, appear to receive carbon from larger trees nearby through the network. Without that help, many of them would probably die, which suggests that a forest behaves less like a collection of competing individuals and more like a community.

There is also evidence that the network carries warnings. In one well-known experiment, researchers allowed aphids to attack the leaves of one plant. Within hours, neighbouring plants connected to it by fungal threads had started producing chemicals which make leaves taste bitter to insects, even though the aphids had never touched them. Plants which were not connected to the first one did not respond in this way.

I should now add a note of caution, because this subject has been popularised, sometimes rather enthusiastically, in books and television programmes, with talk of trees communicating and even looking after their young. Some scientists feel that this goes well beyond the evidence. One criticism is that much of the research has been carried out in greenhouses, where seedlings are grown in pots, rather than in real forests, and conditions in the lab can be very different. Another is that carbon moving through a network does not prove that the transfer benefits the receiving tree, or that it was designed to. So we need to be careful about what we claim.

Even so, the practical implications may be considerable. Forest managers are starting to ask whether the way we treat the soil has been damaging these networks. Ploughing, for example, tears the threads apart, and may explain why young trees planted on cleared land often struggle. If so, then limiting ploughing when replanting a forest might give seedlings a much better chance, and that's a cheap change to make.

To summarise, then. Fungi are neither plants nor trees' enemies, but their closest partners. Their hidden threads feed trees, connect them and perhaps even protect them, though many details are still being debated. Next week, we'll look at how these networks are mapped, and why that is so difficult. Thank you.

passages.title: Stone, timber and time: how the great cathedrals were built
paras: A  Standing beneath the vaulted roof of a medieval cathedral, it is easy to forget that its builders had no cranes powered by engines, no steel and no engineering calculations in the modern sense. Yet between about 1100 and 1500, communities across Europe raised hundreds of stone churches of astonishing height and delicacy. Saint Orlan's Cathedral at Vellmar, begun in 1175 and not completed until 1346, is a typical example: no one who laid its first stone lived to see the last one set in place. Historians have long asked how such projects were organised, paid for and made to stand up.

B  Money came first, and it came slowly. A cathedral was financed by many streams of income rather than by one large grant. The bishop and the clergy contributed a share of their revenues, and wealthy families paid for individual chapels or windows in return for prayers said in their memory. The most reliable source, however, was the pilgrim. A cathedral that owned a famous relic, such as the bone of a local saint, attracted travellers from far away, and their donations paid the masons' wages for years at a time. At Vellmar, the discovery of a saint's tomb in 1201 is thought to have doubled the building fund within a decade. When money ran short, work simply stopped, sometimes for half a century.

C  The person in charge of the work was the master mason, who combined the roles of architect, engineer and site manager. He did not produce detailed plans on paper, for parchment was expensive and drawings were hard to read on a busy site. Instead, he relied on geometry. Using a compass and a straight edge, he worked out the proportions of arches and towers from a few simple ratios, so that the height of a pillar might be fixed as a multiple of its width. Full-size outlines of important stones were scratched into a floor of plaster, and from these the carpenters cut wooden templates, which the stone carvers laid on the blocks. In this way, hundreds of identical pieces could be made by different workers without the master being present.

D  The workforce was large and highly varied. Quarrymen cut the rough stone, often several miles away, and carters or river boats brought it to the town. On site, stone-cutters shaped the blocks, carvers decorated them, and carpenters built the timber frames that held arches in place until the mortar had set. Blacksmiths forged and repaired the iron tools, which became blunt very quickly. Most building took place between spring and autumn, because frost damages fresh mortar, and in winter the labourers were sent to the workshops to prepare stone for the following season. Skilled men were paid by the day, and the accounts that survive suggest that a master carver earned far more than an unskilled labourer.

E  Raising heavy stone to a great height was the most dangerous task of all. The key machine was the treadwheel crane, a large wooden wheel inside which two or three men walked, winding a rope round a drum and lifting loads of up to a tonne. As the walls rose, the crane itself was hauled up to the top of the structure, where it often stayed for decades, and the marks of its fittings can still be seen on some medieval roof timbers. Scaffolds were made of wooden poles lashed together with rope rather than nails. They were light and cheap, but they fell down often, and although accidents must have been common, few were ever recorded.

F  The great technical advance was a set of three connected ideas. The pointed arch carried loads downward more steeply than a round one, which meant that the walls beneath could be thinner. The ribbed vault used slender stone ribs to carry the weight of a lighter infill of stone between them. And the flying buttress, an arch built outside the wall, carried the sideways thrust of the roof to heavy piers away from the building. Together, these allowed builders to open up the walls with large windows filled with coloured glass, so that by the thirteenth century the interior of a cathedral could seem to be made of light rather than stone.

G  Ambition sometimes outran knowledge. In 1284 the vault above the choir of Dunmarrow Cathedral collapsed, probably because its supporting piers were too slender for their height; the townspeople rebuilt it with stronger piers and extra buttresses. Builders had no way of calculating the forces involved, so they learned from experience, and from failures like this one. Even finished cathedrals were rarely left alone: each generation added towers, chapels and windows in the fashion of its day, which is why many look today like a record of several centuries rather than the work of a single mind.

passages.title: Liquid gold that never goes off
paras: A  Archaeologists who open sealed tombs of the ancient world are fond of telling one story. Somewhere, they say, a pot of honey was found among the grave goods, three thousand years old, and still perfectly good to eat. Whether the tale has been polished in the retelling is hard to say, but the principle behind it is sound. Honey, if kept properly, can remain edible for an extraordinarily long time, and no other natural food can quite match it. The explanation lies partly in the bees' remarkable skill as chemists, and partly in the chemistry of honey itself.

B  The raw material is nectar, the sugary liquid produced by flowers to attract insects. Nectar is mostly water, often about four fifths of its weight, and in this form it spoils quickly. A forager bee sucks it up through her tongue and stores it in a special organ, the honey stomach, which is separate from the stomach she uses for her own food. During the flight home, enzymes added by the bee begin to split the main sugar in the nectar, sucrose, into two simpler sugars, glucose and fructose. This is only the start of the process, and it is a laborious one. A single worker will produce no more than a twelfth of a teaspoon of honey in her whole lifetime.

C  Back in the hive, the forager passes her load, mouth to mouth, to younger house bees, which continue to add enzymes and work the nectar for some time. They then deposit droplets in the wax cells of the comb, spreading them in thin layers to increase the surface exposed to the air. The next stage is a collective effort: large numbers of bees stand at the cells and beat their wings, driving a current of warm air through the hive so that water evaporates. When the water content has fallen to roughly eighteen per cent, the bees seal each cell with a lid of wax. The honey is now ready to be stored, in some cases for years.

D  The first reason why honey does not spoil is simply that it is so concentrated. Honey is more than three quarters sugar, and there is so little water left that very few living things can survive in it. This is because of a process called osmosis: when a bacterium or a yeast cell lands in honey, the surrounding sugar draws the water out of it, and the cell dries up. Most microbes need a good deal more water than honey can offer, so they never begin to multiply. Honey is, in effect, too dry a world for them.

E  The second reason is acidity. A further enzyme, added by the bees, converts some of the glucose into a substance called gluconic acid, which gives honey a pH of between about 3.5 and 4.5, roughly as acid as a glass of orange juice. Few bacteria grow well in such conditions. The same enzyme has another effect. When honey is diluted, for example by the fluid from a wound, it releases small amounts of hydrogen peroxide, a mild antiseptic. This is the reason why, for thousands of years, people have spread honey on burns and cuts, and why some hospitals now use specially prepared medical honey on wounds that are slow to heal. Certain varieties, such as those made from a New Zealand shrub, also contain other antibacterial compounds, though scientists are still debating how much they matter.

F  None of this means that honey never changes. Over weeks or months, many kinds slowly turn cloudy and then solid, as the glucose forms crystals. Many shoppers assume that the jar has gone off, but crystallisation is entirely natural and does not affect the safety of the honey; warming the jar gently in a bowl of hot water will turn it back to a liquid. A more serious problem is moisture. Honey is hygroscopic, which means that it absorbs water from the air, and if an open jar is kept somewhere damp, the water content may rise above twenty per cent. At that point, yeasts which have been dormant begin to grow and the honey starts to ferment, producing a sour smell. Beekeepers therefore check the water content of each batch with an instrument called a refractometer before they sell it.

G  Honey is not entirely harmless, however. It should never be given to babies under twelve months, since it can contain spores of a bacterium which an infant's digestive system cannot yet control, and which may cause a rare but serious illness. For adults the spores are no danger. Meanwhile, the sweetness and popularity of honey have created another problem. Because it takes so much effort to produce, genuine honey is expensive, and some dishonest producers have been found to add cheap syrups made from rice or corn. Detecting such fraud is now a growing specialism in food science. Perhaps the most striking recent research, though, looks at honey as a source of new medicines, as researchers search for natural substances that could help to fight bacteria which no longer respond to ordinary antibiotics.

passages.title: Bringing back the lost: should we resurrect extinct species?
paras: A  Every few years, newspapers announce that a long-dead animal is about to walk the earth again. Teams in several countries are working on the woolly mammoth, the passenger pigeon and the Tasmanian tiger, and their press releases speak confidently of resurrection. The word that has stuck, de-extinction, is a flattering one, and the first thing to say is that it is misleading. Nobody can recreate a lost animal exactly. What scientists are attempting to produce is a proxy: a living relative whose genes have been altered to resemble those of the vanished species. A proxy may look like the original and behave a little like it. It will not be the original.

B  The technique is undeniably impressive. DNA is extracted from museum specimens or frozen remains, but it is broken into short fragments and badly damaged, so researchers must reconstruct the missing sections by comparing what survives with the genome of the closest living species. For the mammoth, that species is the Asian elephant. A few dozen genes, perhaps those controlling hair, fat and the ability to tolerate cold, are then edited in the elephant's cells, and an embryo is produced. Yet the genetic work, hard as it is, may not be the greatest obstacle. An embryo must be carried by a mother, and no elephant can safely be asked to bear an animal that no one has ever seen born. Even if it survives, the calf must learn from adults how to find food, where to migrate and how to live in a herd. Such knowledge died with the last members of the species, and it cannot be edited into a genome.

C  Supporters of the idea argue that proxies would do more than satisfy curiosity. Herds of mammoth-like elephants, they say, could restore the vast grasslands of the Arctic. By trampling snow, which acts as insulation, they would allow the winter cold to reach the ground and so slow the thawing of permafrost, which would release enormous quantities of greenhouse gas. It is an arresting proposal, and I do not think it can be dismissed out of hand. But the evidence for it comes largely from one small experiment, in which horses and bison were introduced into a Siberian reserve, and the results cannot simply be scaled up to a continent. Until much more is known, the claim must be regarded as a hope rather than a finding.

D  The financial argument is more straightforward. Conservation budgets are small and the number of species at risk is large. The cost of producing a single proxy, and then keeping a breeding population alive, would be enough to protect many hectares of habitat on which living species depend. It might be replied that the money comes from private investors who would not otherwise spend it on conservation. That may be true in part, but it ignores the more serious danger, which is one of perception. If extinction can be reversed, the public and politicians may come to feel that it is less urgent to prevent. A message that nature can be restored later is a comfortable one, and it is exactly the wrong message to send at a time when species are disappearing faster than at any time in human history.

E  Then there is the question of the animals themselves. The first proxies would be experiments, and experiments fail. Some would be born with defects, and some would not survive. Those that did would probably spend their lives in captivity, and those of a naturally social species, like elephants or passenger pigeons, could be raised without others of their kind. I find it hard to defend a project whose early stages would inevitably involve suffering, when the purpose is not to relieve the suffering of any existing creature but to satisfy the public's appetite for spectacle.

F  Nor is it obvious where the animals would live. The world in which mammoths flourished has largely disappeared, and the passenger pigeon, which once travelled in flocks of millions, needed vast forests and huge numbers of companions to find enough food. A few hundred birds released into modern woodland would be unlikely to survive. The case is stronger for species lost only recently from places that remain largely intact. The Tasmanian tiger, which disappeared in the twentieth century, once lived in forests and grasslands that in many areas still exist, and the habitat that supported it could, in principle, support a proxy again. I would not rule out such a project, but I believe that it would be the exception rather than the rule.

G  If resurrection is a poor reason to pursue this research, is there a better one? I think there is. The same techniques that edit ancient DNA can also be used to help species that are alive today. A North American ferret that had nearly vanished has already produced a healthy clone from cells frozen decades ago, which added to the gene pool of a population that had too little variety to be secure. This kind of genetic rescue, rather than the revival of the mammoth, is the real prize. It is a good reason for the work to continue, provided that the scientists describe it honestly and do not claim more than they can deliver. We should be glad of the science, and wary of the spectacle.
